title: Hub-Spoke Network Topology
summary: A central hub VNet hosts shared services (Azure Firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute Gateway, DNS). Spoke VNets peer to the hub and route all inter-spoke and internet-bound traffic through the hub, enforcing centralized network policy.
whenToUse: Default for almost all Azure deployments. Use for Tier 1 and Tier 2. Migrate to Azure Virtual WAN when managing 5+ spoke VNets or multi-region complexity.
keyDesignDecisions: Force-tunnel all internet-bound traffic through Azure Firewall in the hub
Spoke VNets are non-transitive — spoke-to-spoke requires hub as transit
Hub hosts all Private DNS Zones linked to all spokes
Deploy Azure Bastion in the hub for secure VM access without public IPs

title: Azure Virtual WAN
summary: Microsoft-managed global network backbone that handles transit routing between spoke VNets, branches, and VPN/ExpressRoute circuits. Eliminates manual hub-spoke UDR maintenance at scale.
whenToUse: 5+ spoke VNets, multiple regions, or complex branch connectivity. Preferred over manual hub-spoke at Tier 2+ for its operational simplicity and built-in global routing.
keyDesignDecisions: Standard SKU required for ExpressRoute and VPN coexistence
Each region gets its own Virtual Hub — hubs connect to each other automatically via Microsoft backbone
Secured Virtual Hub = Virtual Hub + Azure Firewall Manager for centralized policy
Any-to-any routing enabled by default between all connections

title: Private Endpoint Strategy
summary: Every PaaS service accessed by production compute uses Private Endpoints, injecting the service NIC into the workload VNet. Public endpoints are disabled via Azure Policy. No PaaS traffic traverses the public internet.
whenToUse: All production Tier 2+; mandatory at Tier 3 and for any regulated workload. Required for FedRAMP, HIPAA, and PCI DSS compliance postures.
keyDesignDecisions: One Private Endpoint resource per PaaS service instance per VNet that needs access
Each Private Endpoint requires a Private DNS Zone A record — automate with Azure Policy (DeployIfNotExists)
Hub-spoke: DNS resolution must flow through the hub's DNS Private Resolver
Budget deployment time: 20-service architecture requires 40+ private endpoint resources

title: SQL Auto-Failover Group
summary: Asynchronous geo-replication between primary and secondary Azure SQL instances across regions with an automated failover listener endpoint. Application connection strings point to the listener DNS name — no code change required on failover.
whenToUse: Relational data requiring RTO < 15 minutes and RPO < 30 minutes. The default choice for production Azure SQL in any multi-region or HA scenario.
keyDesignDecisions: GracePeriodWithDataLossHours must be set explicitly — default is 1 hour which may violate RTO
Use the read-write listener endpoint in connection strings — never connect directly to primary server
Read-only listener can offload read traffic to the secondary during normal operations
Private Endpoints needed in both regions — don't forget the secondary region DNS zone

title: Cosmos DB Multi-Region Writes
summary: Cosmos DB replicates writes to all configured regions simultaneously. Read and write traffic is served from the nearest region. Near-zero RPO and RTO for non-relational data in globally distributed applications.
whenToUse: Non-relational data with near-zero RPO requirement, globally distributed user bases, or any scenario where the 99.999% multi-write SLA is required.
keyDesignDecisions: Configure Last-Write-Wins (LWW) conflict resolution policy — or implement custom merge function
Multi-write increases RU consumption — budget for write amplification across N regions
Consistency level selection: Strong is single-region only; Bounded Staleness or Session for multi-write
Cosmos DB Continuous Backup provides point-in-time restore independent of replication

title: Azure Front Door with WAF
summary: Global HTTP/HTTPS load balancer with built-in WAF (OWASP CRS), TLS offloading, CDN, and automatic failover on origin health probe failure. The default global entry point for internet-facing workloads.
whenToUse: Any internet-facing HTTP/HTTPS workload. Standard SKU for CDN + basic WAF. Premium SKU for advanced WAF rules, private origin connectivity, and bot protection.
keyDesignDecisions: Premium SKU required for private endpoint origins (e.g., App Service with public access disabled)
WAF Policy must be in Prevention mode for production — Detection mode does not block attacks
Custom WAF rules supplement the managed OWASP CRS ruleset — tune exclusions before enabling Prevention
Health probe path must return 200 — configure a dedicated /health endpoint, not the homepage

title: AKS with KEDA and Cluster Autoscaler
summary: AKS cluster with KEDA for event-driven pod scaling (scale-to-zero on queue depth) and Cluster Autoscaler for node-level scaling. Combines cost efficiency (scale-to-zero for idle workloads) with burst capacity.
whenToUse: Microservices with variable load, event-driven processing workloads, or any Tier 2+ architecture where AKS is the compute platform.
azureServices: Azure Service Bus or Event Hubs (scaling source)
keyDesignDecisions: System node pool: 3 nodes across AZs minimum for control plane HA
User node pools: separate from system pool; can scale to zero with KEDA
Pod Disruption Budgets prevent Cluster Autoscaler from removing too many replicas at once
Spot node pools for batch / fault-tolerant workloads — up to 90% cost reduction

title: ExpressRoute + VPN Gateway Coexistence
summary: Deploy both ExpressRoute and VPN Gateway to the same Virtual Network Gateway. ExpressRoute is the primary path; VPN Gateway is the automatic BGP failover path. Provides both high-bandwidth private connectivity and resilient failover.
whenToUse: Tier 2–3 engagements with on-premises integration requirements where ExpressRoute availability or a temporary circuit outage cannot halt operations.
keyDesignDecisions: VPN Gateway must be ErGw1AZ SKU or higher to coexist with ExpressRoute — standard VPN SKU is incompatible
BGP route preference: ExpressRoute routes preferred over VPN routes automatically
ExpressRoute provisioning: 4–8 weeks carrier lead time — start this process in Step 4, not Step 7
MACsec or IPSec over ExpressRoute required for regulated workloads (ExpressRoute is not encrypted by default)
